context.setting: Publicans and sinners were drawing near to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes murmured, “This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them” (Luke 15:1–2). Jesus answered with parables of a lost sheep, a lost piece of silver, and two sons. In verses 11–16 the younger son asks for his portion, wastes it in a far country, and ends up feeding swine, hungry.
context.speaker: Jesus Christ, telling a parable
context.audience: Pharisees and scribes who murmured, while publicans and sinners drew near to hear (Luke 15:1–3)

themes.note: The son ‘came to himself,’ decided to return, and confessed: “Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight.”

Jesus told this parable soon after saying “joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth.” Many readers see that joy pictured in the father's welcome and celebration; the parable leaves the comparison to the listener.
The father receives him as a son, with a robe, a ring, shoes, and a feast. The servant's place the son planned to ask for never comes up.

keyPhrases.meaning: A turning point: he sees his situation clearly. The footnote links the phrase to the Topical Guide entry ‘Repent.’ Repentance is “A change of mind and heart that brings a fresh attitude toward God, oneself, and life in general.”

keyPhrases.phrase: I will arise and go to my father
keyPhrases.meaning: He decides, and then acts on it: verse 20 says “he arose, and came to his father.”

keyPhrases.phrase: I have sinned against heaven, and before thee
keyPhrases.meaning: ‘Against heaven’ is commonly read as meaning against God, alongside the wrong done to his father (‘before thee’). That is an interpretation; the parable doesn't explain the phrase. The footnote on ‘sinned’ points to the Topical Guide entry Confession.

keyPhrases.phrase: make me as one of thy hired servants
keyPhrases.meaning: He plans to ask only for a servant's place. When he meets his father (verse 21), he doesn't say this part.

keyPhrases.phrase: when he was yet a great way off
keyPhrases.meaning: The father sees him while he is still far away, and goes to meet him before he arrives.
The Guide to the Scriptures says compassion means literally “to suffer with,” and also to show “sympathy, pity, and mercy for another.”
The father gives the best robe, a ring, and shoes: far more than the servant's place the son meant to ask for.

keyPhrases.phrase: he was lost, and is found
keyPhrases.meaning: The same words close the parable (verse 32) and echo the lost sheep: “I have found my sheep which was lost.”

related.note: The beginning of the story: the younger son asks for his portion, wastes it “with riotous living,” and is left feeding swine.
The parable of the lost sheep ends, “joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth.”
The elder son is angry and won't go in. The father goes out to him too: “therefore came his father out, and entreated him.”
Alma testifies that “the arms of mercy are extended towards them, and he saith: Repent, and I will receive you.”

questions.question: Who was Jesus talking to when He told this parable?
questions.answer: Luke 15:1–2 says “all the publicans and sinners” drew near to hear Him, and “the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them.” The parables that follow, including this one, answer that complaint.

questions.question: Does the father stand for Heavenly Father?
questions.answer: Jesus doesn't say so directly. Many readers understand the father's welcome as a picture of God's love, because the parable of the lost sheep, told just before, ends with “joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth” (Luke 15:7). A parable is “A simple story used to illustrate and teach a spiritual truth or principle” (Guide to the Scriptures). This one leaves the comparison for the listener to draw.

questions.question: Why is the son's speech in verse 21 shorter than the one he planned in verses 18–19?
questions.answer: In verse 19 he planned to say, “make me as one of thy hired servants.” In verse 21 he says only the first part, and then the father speaks to his servants: “Bring forth the best robe.” The text doesn't say why the request is missing or whether the father interrupted him. What it shows is the father's answer: he receives him as a son.

connections.note: The son comes to himself, returns to his father, and confesses.
Many readers see the father's welcome as a picture of the joy in heaven the Savior described (Luke 15:7); the parable leaves that comparison to the listener.

verses.text: And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!
I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee,
And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants.
And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
And the son said unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son.
But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet:
And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry:
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.
Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him.
And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them.
¶ And he said, A certain man had two sons:
And the younger of them said to his father, Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth to me. And he divided unto them his living.
And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.
And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want.
And he went and joined himself to a citizen of that country; and he sent him into his fields to feed swine.
And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him.
What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?
And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
And when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost.
I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.
And he was angry, and would not go in: therefore came his father out, and entreated him.

And he answering said to his father, Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment: and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends:
But as soon as this thy son was come, which hath devoured thy living with harlots, thou hast killed for him the fatted calf.
And he said unto him, Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine.
It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.
Behold, he sendeth an invitation unto all men, for the arms of mercy are extended towards them, and he saith: Repent, and I will receive you.

notes.resolution: Resolved: confirmed. Luke 15:11–24 is 14 verses; the passage is Luke 15:17–24 (8 verses), and Luke 15:11–16 is declared and shown as a related source (‘leads-to’).

notes.note: Linking the father to God's love is interpretive. It rests on the setting (Luke 15:7, 10), and the text is careful to say the parable leaves the comparison to the listener. Please review.
notes.resolution: Qualified: the answer, the love-of-god theme note, and the Map connection now say that linking the father to God's love is how many readers understand the parable, and that the parable leaves the comparison to the listener. The answer now cites only Luke 15:7, whose words it quotes (verse 10 is worded differently). The forgiveness theme, the hired-servants meaning, the speech-changes answer, and the sort item no longer imply the father interrupted his son.
